Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "The dynamic assembly of distinct RNA polymerase I complexes modulates rDNA transcription" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Kevin Struhl as the Senior Editor, Alan Hinnebusch as the Reviewing Editor and two reviewers.

The majority of the remaining issues have been raised by the Reviewing editor, as described below:

The authors have substantially improved the manuscript in several respects to address all of the major criticisms. They obtained a new mutation in the A43 CTT that specifically impairs homodimerization without affecting interaction with Rrn3, and showed that this mutation dampened the loss of Pol I:Rrn3 complexes from promoter DNA in starved cells, thereby providing evidence that dimerization is an important component of the down-regulation of Pol I recruitment and transcription. They better explained the partial cleft closure observed in their cryoEM structure of the Pol I monomer. They provided evidence that the A14 deletion does not simply destabilize Pol I as the means of impairing complex formation with Rrn3 and promoter binding of the complex. Importantly, they also added additional mutants that implicate helix 2 of the A14 subunit in Rrn3 association with Pol I, exploiting novel predictions of their Pol I:Rrn3 structure. They have also better explained the quantification of results from the PICT assay. As such, there are no remaining major criticisms that would require any additional experimentation to address.

However, there are two major issues with their description of the results.

First, their description of the new coIP experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 is very confusing and incomplete. The only results that are straightforward are shown in lanes 1-2 and 5-6, which provide valuable evidence for Pol I homodimers in the soluble fractions obtained from cross-linked cells when the cells have been starved. In their "Responses to reviewers", they provide a somewhat more complete explanation of the last 3 lanes pertaining to the insoluble cell fractions, but even this doesn't make complete sense, and it was left out of the manuscript/legends completely. A coherent explanation of all of the lanes in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 is required.

Second, in the Discussion: the statement that "initial transcriptional inactivation is mainly driven by Pol I:Rrn3 disassembly." does not seem justified. The experiments in Figure 4A-B clearly show that the bulk of the dissociation of Pol I: Rrn3 from the promoter occurs within the first 20 min at a timepoint where Pol I:Rrn3 complexes are still very abundant and almost no Pol I homodimers have formed. It seems unavoidable that there is another regulatory mechanism apart from dissociation of Pol I:Rrn3 complexes and Pol I homodimerization responsible for the rapid and nearly complete loss of promoter-bound Pol I on starvation. From their statements at several places in the text, it appears that the authors actually agree with this view, but they don't state it directly in the Discussion and it is not depicted in the final model, which could be misleading to the field. The authors are urged to acknowledge more explicating in the Discussion and in their final model that there remains an important gap in knowledge about how the rapid dissociation of the Pol I:Rrn3 complex from the promoter is achieved on starvation.

Reviewer #2:

My major criticisms of the original manuscript concerned the use of the PICT technique and more precisely the analysis of images. The authors have tried to address these concerns, but it is clear that their quantification of Pol1 dimer and Pol1-Rrn3 complex formation is subject to considerable noise. This said, they now provide a detailed quantification protocol and have attempted to better explain the steps used to eliminate problems caused by the very high and variable GFP background signal. They have also improved their ChIP data, clearly validating their ChIP signal for Rrn3.

Given the novelty of the approach and the importance of better understanding Pol1 dimerization and whether or not it has a regulatory role, I feel that on balance the data should now be published.

Reviewer #3:

The revised version of this manuscript does a much better job explaining the PICT assay, and now that I understand how to look at the data I find that the authors have made a persuasive case. These experiments are very important in showing that yeast RNA pol I uses controlled dimerization, in competition with Rrn3 binding, to regulate transcription in response to nutrients and translational status. This work is nicely complemented by some structures that confirm and extend recent work from other groups. I am in favor of publication in eLife.

claims.source: We present in vivo evidence that, when growth is arrested by nutrient deprivation, cells induce rapid clearance of Pol I–Rrn3 complexes, followed by the assembly of inactive Pol I homodimers.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript using PICT assays and other techniques.

claims.claim: Nutrient deprivation is followed by the assembly of inactive Pol I homodimers.
claims.source: We present in vivo evidence that, when growth is arrested by nutrient deprivation, cells induce rapid clearance of Pol I–Rrn3 complexes, followed by the assembly of inactive Pol I homodimers.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PICT assays and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claims.claim: The dual repressive mechanism of Pol I–Rrn3 clearance and Pol I homodimerization reverts upon nutrient addition, thus restoring cell growth.
claims.source: This dual repressive mechanism reverts upon nutrient addition, thus restoring cell growth.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-course experiments showing the dynamics of Pol I complexes in response to nutrient availability.

claims.claim: Pol I dimers form after inhibition of ribosome biogenesis.
claims.source: Moreover, Pol I dimers also form after inhibition of either ribosome biogenesis or protein synthesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using diazaborine to inhibit ribosome biogenesis.

claims.claim: Pol I dimers form after inhibition of protein synthesis.
claims.source: Moreover, Pol I dimers also form after inhibition of either ribosome biogenesis or protein synthesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using cycloheximide to inhibit protein synthesis.

claims.claim: Subunits A43 and A14 play a central role in the regulation of differential Pol I complexes assembly and subsequent promoter association.
claims.source: Our mutational analysis, based on the electron cryomicroscopy structures of monomeric Pol I alone and in complex with Rrn3, underscores the central role of subunits A43 and A14 in the regulation of differential Pol I complexes assembly and subsequent promoter association.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mutational analysis combined with structural data from cryo-EM.

claims.claim: Pol I retains up to 60% of the total transcriptional activity within the eukaryotic nucleus in actively growing cells.
claims.source: The critical requirement for ribosomes in actively growing cells causes that Pol I retains up to 60% of the total transcriptional activity within the eukaryotic nucleus (Warner, 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Warner, 1999.

claims.claim: Under stress conditions, cells tune down ribosome biosynthesis by repressing Pol I transcription.
claims.source: However, under stress conditions, cells tune down ribosome biosynthesis by repressing Pol I transcription (Mayer et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mayer et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Defects in the regulation of Pol I transcription can lead to uncontrolled cell proliferation and have been associated with different types of cancer.
claims.source: Accordingly, defects in the regulation of this process can lead to uncontrolled cell proliferation and have been associated with different types of cancer (Bywater et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bywater et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Rrn3 binding to Pol I is a prerequisite for enzyme recruitment to promoter-bound initiation factors in yeast.
claims.source: While the first three components recognize different regions in promoter DNA, Rrn3 binding to Pol I is a prerequisite for enzyme recruitment to promoter-bound initiation factors (Keener et al., 1998; Yamamoto et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Keener et al., 1998 and Yamamoto et al., 1996.

claims.claim: Yeast Pol I is a 590 kDa enzyme composed of 14 subunits.
claims.source: Yeast Pol I is a 590 kDa enzyme composed of 14 subunits, whose atomic architecture was recently revealed (Engel et al., 2013; Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies by Engel et al., 2013 and Fernández-Tornero et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The A43 C-terminal tail is important to maintain Pol I dimers.
claims.source: The structure suggests that the interaction between the A43 C-terminal tail and the opposite monomer's clamp is important to maintain Pol I dimers.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the crystal structure of Pol I dimers.

claims.claim: Pol I dimers in solution present the same structural arrangement as in the crystal structure.
claims.source: Interestingly, Pol I dimers in solution present the same structural arrangement, as shown by cryo-EM (Pilsl et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pilsl et al., 2016.

claims.claim: No evidence was available prior to this study showing Pol I dimers to exist within the cell.
claims.source: While homodimerization has been proposed as a potential regulatory mechanism of Pol I activity, no evidence is available to date showing Pol I dimers to exist within the cell.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the existing literature at the time of the study.

claims.claim: The Tub4-RFP-FKBP anchor increases PICT sensitivity by up to 200-fold compared to previously-engineered anchors.
claims.source: The resulting cells harbour only one or two anchors, thus increasing the PICT sensitivity by up to 200-fold (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the new anchor to previous anchors.

claims.claim: Cells incubated in rich medium present normal growth rate and the vast majority of Pol I accumulates in a sub-nuclear structure likely corresponding to the nucleolus.
claims.source: Cells incubated in rich medium present normal growth rate and the vast majority of Pol I accumulates in a sub-nuclear structure likely corresponding to the nucleolus (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data and inference about the identity of the sub-nuclear structure.

claims.claim: Upon rapamycin addition in rich medium, no recruitment of A190-GFP could be detected at the anchors.
claims.source: Upon rapamycin addition, no recruitment of A190-GFP could be detected at the anchors (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PICT assay data showing no Pol I homodimerization in growing cells.

claims.claim: When cells were incubated in starving medium, their growth was arrested and A190-GFP translocated to the nuclear side of the anchors.
claims.source: In contrast, when cells were incubated in a medium lacking carbon and nitrogen, hereafter starving medium, their growth was arrested and A190-GFP translocated to the nuclear side of the anchors (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PICT assay data showing Pol I homodimerization in starved cells.

claims.claim: The total levels of A190 as well as the distribution of A190-GFP in the anchor vicinity prior to rapamycin addition are equivalent in both rich and starving media.
claims.source: Interestingly, the total levels of A190 as well as the distribution of A190-GFP in the anchor vicinity prior to rapamycin addition are equivalent in both media (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and microscopy data.

claims.claim: Pol I homodimers are only detected in the soluble fraction of starved cells.
claims.source: Analysis of the soluble fraction showed that Pol I homodimers are only detected in starved cells (lanes 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from fractionated cell extracts.

claims.claim: The chromatin insoluble fraction of growing cells presented high levels of A190-MYC, likely corresponding to rDNA-associated Pol I molecules.
claims.source: As expected, the chromatin insoluble fraction of growing cells presented high levels of A190-MYC (lane 7), likely corresponding to rDNA-associated Pol I molecules, while tiny amounts of A190-MYC were detected for starved cells (lane 8).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data and inference about the identity of chromatin-associated Pol I.

claims.claim: The A43 C-terminal tail is essential for Pol I homodimerization.
claims.source: In this mutant, Pol I homodimerization is impaired (Figure 1B), confirming the observation derived from structural data.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PICT assay data from the A43ΔCt mutant and structural data.

claims.claim: Pol III does not dimerize in growing or starving conditions.
claims.source: In the case of Pol III, no oligomerization was observed on the anchor in either growing or starving medium, indicating that Pol III does not dimerize in these conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PICT assay data for Pol III.

claims.claim: No additional protein synthesis is required to induce Pol I homodimerization upon starvation.
claims.source: This indicates that no additional protein synthesis is required to induce this cellular event and that ribosome inhibition could reinforce Pol I dimerization (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using cycloheximide in starved cells.

claims.claim: Ribosome inhibition could reinforce Pol I dimerization.
claims.source: This indicates that no additional protein synthesis is required to induce this cellular event and that ribosome inhibition could reinforce Pol I dimerization (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the observation of increased Pol I homodimerization in the presence of cycloheximide and involves speculative reasoning.

claims.claim: Inhibition of protein synthesis in cells grown in non-starving medium is sufficient to induce Pol I dimerization.
claims.source: Interestingly, inhibition of protein synthesis in cells grown in non-starving medium was sufficient to induce Pol I dimerization (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PICT assay data using cycloheximide in growing cells.

claims.claim: Pol I homodimerization is induced by inhibition of rRNA maturation.
claims.source: When cycloheximide was replaced by diazaborine, an inhibitor of rRNA maturation during 60S formation (Loibl et al., 2014), Pol I dimers were also assembled (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PICT assay data using diazaborine and a citation to Loibl et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Pol I homodimerization is induced by inhibition of processes that are downstream of rRNA synthesis.
claims.source: These results show that Pol I homodimerization is induced by inhibition of either protein synthesis or rRNA maturation, two processes that are downstream of rRNA synthesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results with cycloheximide and diazaborine.

claims.claim: The levels of Pol I–Rrn3 complexes are reduced to about 40% upon nutrient deprivation.
claims.source: Despite Pol I–Rrn3 complexes were detected in cells incubated in both rich and starving media, their levels were reduced to about 40% upon nutrient deprivation (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PICT assay data comparing Pol I–Rrn3 levels in rich and starving media.

claims.claim: The cellular levels of Rrn3-GFP drop significantly in starved cells.
claims.source: Importantly, while starvation does not induce significant changes in the distribution of Rrn3-GFP in the vicinity of the anchor (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), the cellular levels of Rrn3-GFP drop significantly in starved cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing reduced Rrn3 levels in starved cells.

claims.claim: The reduction in Rrn3 and Pol I–Rrn3 correlates with an almost complete deprivation of both Pol I and Rrn3 from rDNA promoters.
claims.source: The reduction in Rrn3 and Pol I–Rrn3 correlates with an almost complete deprivation of both Pol I and Rrn3 from rDNA promoters, as observed by ChIP experiments (Figure 3C–D, wt-35S).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data showing reduced promoter occupancy in starved cells.

claims.claim: A43ΔCt cells present reduced growth compared to wild-type cells.
claims.source: For that, we constructed A43ΔCt haploid cells that, while expressing similar levels of Rrn3 and A190 to wild-type cells, present reduced growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by growth phenotype data comparing A43ΔCt to wild-type.

claims.claim: The A43 C-terminal tail is not involved in Rrn3 binding.
claims.source: Structural data show that the A43 C-terminal tail is not involved in Rrn3 binding (see below; Engel et al., 2016; Pilsl et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from this study and citations to Engel et al., 2016 and Pilsl et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Growing A43ΔCt cells exhibit levels of Pol I–Rrn3 complexes equivalent to the wild-type.
claims.source: Growing A43ΔCt cells exhibit levels of Pol I–Rrn3 complexes equivalent to the wild-type (Figure 3B), whereas Pol I promoter association is slightly increased (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PICT assay and ChIP data comparing A43ΔCt to wild-type in growing conditions.

claims.claim: In starved A43ΔCt cells, the levels of Pol I–Rrn3 complexes are about 2-fold higher than those detected in wild-type cells.
claims.source: More interestingly, in starved A43ΔCt cells, the levels of Pol I–Rrn3 complexes are about 2-fold higher than those detected in wild-type cells (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PICT assay data comparing A43ΔCt to wild-type in starving conditions.

claims.claim: In starved A43ΔCt cells, association of Pol I along the rDNA gene and of Rrn3 at the promoter increase about 6-fold with respect to the wild-type.
claims.source: Furthermore, in these conditions, association of Pol I along the rDNA gene and of Rrn3 at the promoter increase about 6-fold with respect to the wild-type (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data comparing A43ΔCt to wild-type in starving conditions.

claims.claim: Pol I homodimerization is important for complete Pol I–Rrn3 clearance and transcription inactivation upon starvation.
claims.source: Overall, our results indicate that Pol I homodimerization is important for complete Pol I–Rrn3 clearance and transcription inactivation upon starvation.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results with A43ΔCt and CARA mutants.

claims.claim: Detected levels of Pol I–Rrn3 are rapidly depleted by about 30% within the first 15 minutes when growing cells are transferred to starving medium.
claims.source: When growing cells are transferred to starving medium, detected levels of Pol I–Rrn3 are rapidly depleted by about 30%, in a process that follows an exponential decay (Figure 4A, left).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-course PICT assay data.

claims.claim: Pol I homodimers remain undetectable within the first 15 minutes of starvation.
claims.source: Accordingly, the rate of complex clearance is maximal within the first 15 min, while Pol I homodimers remain undetectable at this stage.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-course PICT assay data.

claims.claim: A symmetric pattern is observed when starved cells are transferred to nutrient rich medium.
claims.source: A symmetric pattern is observed when starved cells are transferred to nutrient rich medium (Figure 4A, right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-course PICT assay data showing the reversal of Pol I complex dynamics upon refeeding.

claims.claim: The overall levels of A190 remain constant during starvation and refeeding.
claims.source: Western-blot analysis at the same time-points shows that the overall levels of A190 remain constant while those of Rrn3 correlate with detected amounts of Pol I–Rrn3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Rrn3 levels influence the number of Pol I–Rrn3 complexes, as previously proposed (Philippi et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data from time-course experiments.

claims.claim: Rrn3 levels influence the number of Pol I–Rrn3 complexes.
claims.source: Western-blot analysis at the same time-points shows that the overall levels of A190 remain constant while those of Rrn3 correlate with detected amounts of Pol I–Rrn3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Rrn3 levels influence the number of Pol I–Rrn3 complexes, as previously proposed (Philippi et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation between Rrn3 levels and Pol I–Rrn3 complex levels, and is supported by a citation to Philippi et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Cells respond to nutrient availability by differentially adjusting the levels of Pol I homodimers and Pol I–Rrn3.
claims.source: Overall, these results indicate that cells respond to nutrient availability by differentially adjusting the levels of Pol I homodimers and Pol I–Rrn3.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the time-course data showing different dynamics for the two types of complexes.

claims.claim: The cryo-EM structure of monomeric Pol I was determined at 4.9 Å resolution.
claims.source: Finally, the addition of both particle sets followed by 3D refinement yielded a map that is virtually identical to that of monomeric Pol I but reaches a resolution of 4.9 Å (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, central), thus allowing the building of a quasi-atomic model (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data and structural analysis.

claims.claim: The cryo-EM structure of the Pol I–Rrn3 complex was determined at 7.7 Å resolution.
claims.source: Refinement of the second group, containing an extra piece of density next to the Pol I stalk that corresponds to Rrn3, produced a 7.7 Å resolution map (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, left).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data and structural analysis.

claims.claim: The Pol I stalk appears almost completely disordered in monomeric Pol I.
claims.source: The Pol I stalk appears almost completely disordered, in spite of weak density at the region directly contacting the enzyme core, i.e. the tip domain in subunit A43 (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM structural data showing lack of density for the stalk.

claims.claim: The stalk is highly dynamic in monomeric Pol I, which may be important in the Pol I activation process.
claims.source: This indicates that the stalk is highly dynamic, which may be important in the Pol I activation process.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the structural observation of stalk disorder and involves speculation about its functional importance.

claims.claim: The cleft entrance in monomeric Pol I is 38 Å in width.
claims.source: The resulting cleft entrance is 38 Å in width, which leaves enough room for double stranded DNA to access the bottom of the cleft.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural measurements from the cryo-EM map.

claims.claim: The cleft in monomeric Pol I is about half way from inactive dimeric to elongating Pol I.
claims.source: While further cleft closure is required to reach a transcription-competent state (Neyer et al., 2016; Tafur et al., 2016), the cleft in monomeric Pol I is about half way from inactive dimeric to elongating Pol I.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from structural comparisons and is supported by citations to Neyer et al., 2016 and Tafur et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Rrn3 binds Pol I with its N-terminus facing the stalk.
claims.source: Antibody labelling confirms that this density corresponds to Rrn3, which binds Pol I with its N-terminus facing the stalk (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by antibody labeling experiments and structural analysis.

claims.claim: Rrn3 binding fixes the Pol I stalk with respect to free monomeric Pol I.
claims.source: Interestingly, Rrn3 binding fixes the Pol I stalk with respect to free monomeric Pol I, thus generating a surface for interaction with promoter-bound initiation factors (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison between monomeric Pol I and the Pol I–Rrn3 complex.

claims.claim: The conformation of the enzyme in the Pol I–Rrn3 complex is virtually identical to that of monomeric Pol I.
claims.source: Apart from stalk ordering, the conformation of the enzyme in the Pol I–Rrn3 complex is virtually identical to that of monomeric Pol I, indicating that conformational changes are not associated with Rrn3 binding.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison between monomeric Pol I and the Pol I–Rrn3 complex.

claims.claim: Conformational changes are not associated with Rrn3 binding to Pol I.
claims.source: Apart from stalk ordering, the conformation of the enzyme in the Pol I–Rrn3 complex is virtually identical to that of monomeric Pol I, indicating that conformational changes are not associated with Rrn3 binding.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the structural comparison showing no major conformational changes upon Rrn3 binding.

claims.claim: The A43 subunit strongly binds Rrn3 HEAT repeats H2-H4.
claims.source: The A43 subunit strongly binds Rrn3 HEAT repeats H2-H4, through interaction surfaces of both proteins that contain several serine residues.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of the Pol I–Rrn3 interface.

claims.claim: S145 in Rrn3 falls at the heart of a serine cradle in the A43 OB domain formed by residues S141, S143, S156 and S244.
claims.source: In particular S145 in Rrn3, whose phosphomimetic mutant exhibits a growth defect (Blattner et al., 2011), falls at the heart of a serine cradle in the A43 OB domain formed by residues S141, S143, S156 and S244 (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and a citation to Blattner et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The second stalk subunit, A14, contacts Rrn3 around HEAT repeat H5 using helix α2 of its tip-associated (TA) domain.
claims.source: The second stalk subunit, A14, contacts Rrn3 around HEAT repeat H5 using helix α2 of its tip-associated (TA) domain.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of the Pol I–Rrn3 interface.

claims.claim: ΔA14 cells exhibit a 75% decrease in Pol I–Rrn3 as compared to wild-type.
claims.source: In agreement with cryo-EM data, ΔA14 cells exhibit a 75% decrease in Pol I–Rrn3 as compared to wild-type (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PICT assay data from the ΔA14 mutant.

claims.claim: A14 plays a role in Pol I association to rDNA.
claims.source: These results indicate that A14 plays a role in Pol I association to rDNA.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ΔA14 mutant data showing reduced promoter association.

claims.claim: The A14 C-terminal tail is not involved in Rrn3 binding.
claims.source: A strain lacking the C-terminal tail (A14ΔCt, Δ101–137) presents similar levels of Pol I–Rrn3 and promoter association as wild-type cells (Figure 7F), indicating that the A14 C-terminal tail is not involved in Rrn3 binding.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PICT assay and ChIP data from the A14ΔCt mutant.

claims.claim: Helix α2 in A14 is fundamental for Rrn3 binding and subsequent promoter association.
claims.source: Our A14 mutational analysis indicates that helix α2 is fundamental for Rrn3 binding and subsequent promoter association.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the mutational analysis of A14 helix α2.

claims.claim: The TA-loop in A14 has a role in limiting binding to Rrn3.
claims.source: This suggests that the TA-loop in A14 has a role in limiting binding to Rrn3.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the A14ΔTAloop mutant data showing increased Pol I–Rrn3 levels.

claims.claim: Higher levels of Pol I–Rrn3 are not sufficient to influence Pol I homodimerization or promoter dissociation in starved cells.
claims.source: These data also show that higher levels of Pol I–Rrn3 are not sufficient to influence Pol I homodimerization or promoter dissociation in starved cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the A14ΔTAloop mutant data in starving conditions.

claims.claim: The formation of compact homodimers could protect a pool of Pol I from degradation, thus saving energy to the cell.
claims.source: On one hand, the formation of compact homodimers could protect a pool of this highly-abundant enzyme from degradation, thus saving energy to the cell.
claims.evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning about the functional advantage of Pol I dimerization.

claims.claim: Upon restoration of favourable conditions, rRNA synthesis can be reactivated from stored Pol I dimers, while de novo Pol I production would delay the process.
claims.source: On the other hand, upon restoration of favourable conditions, rRNA synthesis can be reactivated, while de novo Pol I production would delay the process, especially if few ribosomes are available.
claims.evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning about the functional advantage of Pol I dimerization.

claims.claim: Homodimerization is not a general mechanism to regulate eukaryotic transcription.
claims.source: Finally, although we cannot exclude that Pol II or Pol III could homodimerize in conditions other than nutrient starvation, our results suggest that homodimerization is not a general mechanism to regulate eukaryotic transcription.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that Pol II and Pol III do not dimerize under the tested conditions.

claims.claim: Only a minor fraction of Pol I is bound to Rrn3 in growing cells.
claims.source: While only a minor fraction of Pol I is bound to Rrn3 in growing cells (Milkereit and Tschochner, 1998), the formation of this complex is a pre-requisite for transcription initiation (Aprikian et al., 2001; Schnapp et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Milkereit and Tschochner, 1998.

claims.claim: The formation of the Pol I–Rrn3 complex is a pre-requisite for transcription initiation.
claims.source: While only a minor fraction of Pol I is bound to Rrn3 in growing cells (Milkereit and Tschochner, 1998), the formation of this complex is a pre-requisite for transcription initiation (Aprikian et al., 2001; Schnapp et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aprikian et al., 2001 and Schnapp et al., 1993.

claims.claim: Pol I–Rrn3 levels as such are not sufficient to account for transcription inactivation by nutrient depletion.
claims.source: However, the levels of Pol I–Rrn3 as such are not sufficient to account for transcription inactivation by nutrient depletion, as Pol I–Rrn3 complexes can be detected regardless of null promoter levels of A190 and Rrn3.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that Pol I–Rrn3 complexes persist even when promoter occupancy is negligible.

claims.claim: Both Pol I–Rrn3 and Pol I dimerization modulate rDNA transcription.
claims.source: Therefore, both Pol I–Rrn3 and Pol I dimerization modulate rDNA transcription, which allows us to propose a model (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined data on Pol I–Rrn3 clearance and Pol I dimerization.

claims.claim: Additional regulatory mechanisms may contribute to initial transcriptional inactivation upon starvation.
claims.source: We thus hypothesize that, in addition to Pol I–Rrn3 disassembly, additional regulatory mechanisms may contribute to initial transcriptional inactivation.
claims.evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning based on the observation that Pol I–Rrn3 complexes persist despite low promoter occupancy.

claims.claim: Available Pol I–Rrn3 complexes are rapidly recruited for transcription upon refeeding from starvation.
claims.source: Upon refeeding from starvation, we propose that available Pol I–Rrn3 complexes are rapidly recruited for transcription, while disruption of Pol I homodimers provides fresh Pol I that can interact with Rrn3 to increase Pol I–Rrn3 complexes and further activate rDNA transcription.
claims.evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning based on the observed dynamics of Pol I complexes upon refeeding.

claims.claim: The A43 C-terminal tail is conserved from yeast to human.
claims.source: The A43 C-terminal tail is conserved from yeast to human, arguing for a Pol I monomer/dimer modulation of rRNA synthesis in higher eukaryotes (Beckouët et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beckouët et al., 2011.

claims.claim: There are organisms lacking the A43 C-terminal tail, such as S. pombe and A. thaliana, where likely no Pol I dimerization will take place in nutrient-arrested cells.
claims.source: Nevertheless, there are organisms lacking the A43 C-terminal tail, such as S. pombe and A. thaliana, where likely no Pol I dimerization will take place in nutrient-arrested cells.
claims.evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning based on the absence of the A43 C-terminal tail in certain organisms.

claims.claim: The main Pol I element involved in Rrn3 interaction is the OB domain in the A43 elongated core.
claims.source: Additionally, our cryo-EM structure shows that the main Pol I element involved in Rrn3 interaction is the OB domain in the A43 elongated core.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of the Pol I–Rrn3 interface.

claims.claim: The interaction between A43 and Rrn3 can only take place if Pol I is phosphorylated and Rrn3 is not.
claims.source: In agreement, it was shown that this interaction can only take place if Pol I is phosphorylated and Rrn3 is not (Fath et al., 2001; Gerber et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fath et al., 2001 and Gerber et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Three structural elements in Pol I are involved in the interaction with Rrn3: the stalk, the dock domain, and the AC40/AC19 heterodimer.
claims.source: Three structural elements in Pol I are involved in the interaction with Rrn3: (i) the stalk, (ii) the dock domain, and (iii) the AC40/AC19 heterodimer.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of the Pol I–Rrn3 interface.

claims.claim: Contact of the activating factor with the stalk, dock domain, and AC40/AC19 heterodimer is required for activation and subsequent binding to promoter-attached initiation factors.
claims.source: Contact of the activating factor with these three regions is therefore required for activation and subsequent binding to promoter-attached initiation factors.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the structural data showing these interaction sites.

claims.claim: The Mediator complex acts as an activating cofactor required for association of Pol II to promoter-bound initiation factors.
claims.source: In the Pol II system, the Mediator complex acts as an activating cofactor required for association of the enzyme to promoter-bound initiation factors (Kim et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 1994.

claims.claim: The Pol II–Mediator structure shows that the coactivator contacts the enzyme at the stalk, the dock domain, and the AC40/AC19 homolog.
claims.source: Interestingly, the Pol II–Mediator structure shows that the coactivator contacts the enzyme at the stalk, the dock domain, and the AC40/AC19 homolog (Plaschka et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Plaschka et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The interaction of activating factors with the stalk and surrounding regions might help bring RNA polymerases to the promoter.
claims.source: While other details of the enzyme-cofactor interaction differ between both transcription systems (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), the described similarities suggest that the interaction of activating factors with the stalk and surrounding regions might help bring RNA polymerases to the promoter.
claims.evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning based on the structural similarities between Pol I–Rrn3 and Pol II–Mediator.

claims.claim: Domain 4 of the σ factor (σ4) falls in the region where Rrn3 is located and contacts equivalent domains of the RNA polymerase core.
claims.source: Fitting of the bacterial holoenzyme structure into our cryo-EM map shows that domain 4 of the σ factor (σ4) falls in the region where Rrn3 is located and contacts equivalent domains of the RNA polymerase core (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison between the Pol I–Rrn3 complex and the bacterial holoenzyme.

claims.claim: σ4 binds the bacterial promoter DNA.
claims.source: Moreover, σ4 binds the bacterial promoter DNA (Murakami et al., 2002) and mammalian Rrn3 was shown to interact with the rDNA promoter (Stepanchick et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Murakami et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Mammalian Rrn3 was shown to interact with the rDNA promoter.
claims.source: Moreover, σ4 binds the bacterial promoter DNA (Murakami et al., 2002) and mammalian Rrn3 was shown to interact with the rDNA promoter (Stepanchick et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stepanchick et al., 2013.

claims.claim: An overall architectural arrangement may be conserved to mediate enzyme activation and promoter recruitment across different transcription systems.
claims.source: These analogies suggest that an overall architectural arrangement may be conserved to mediate enzyme activation and promoter recruitment.
claims.evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning based on the structural similarities observed across different transcription systems.

results.result: Nutrient deprivation induces formation of Pol I homodimers in vivo, which are detected in the soluble fraction of starved cells but not in growing cells. The A43 C-terminal tail is essential for this dimerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 provide converging evidence from PICT assays, co-immunoprecipitation, and mutational analysis. The A43ΔCt mutant specifically abolishes dimerization (C24) while maintaining equivalent protein levels (C21), confirming the structural prediction (C14). Controls show no dimerization in growing cells (C19) and proper fractionation (C22-C23).

results.result: Pol I homodimerization is induced by inhibition of processes downstream of rRNA synthesis, including protein synthesis (cycloheximide) and rRNA maturation (diazaborine), and does not require new protein synthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C29 demonstrate that Pol I dimerization occurs with cycloheximide and diazaborine treatment in both starved and growing cells. The observation that cycloheximide doesn't prevent dimerization in starved cells (C26) establishes that no new protein synthesis is required. The inference that these represent downstream effects (C30) is reasonable given the known mechanisms of these inhibitors.

results.result: Nutrient deprivation causes rapid clearance of Pol I-Rrn3 complexes (reduced to ~40%) and near-complete loss of Pol I and Rrn3 from rDNA promoters. This clearance follows exponential decay kinetics with maximal rate in the first 15 minutes, preceding Pol I dimerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 establish the reduction in Pol I-Rrn3 levels and promoter occupancy using PICT and ChIP. Time-course data (C40-C41) demonstrate the temporal sequence where Pol I-Rrn3 clearance precedes dimerization. Western blot data (C43) shows constant A190 levels while Rrn3 decreases, supporting the correlation with complex levels (C44). The differential dynamics (C45) are well-documented.

results.result: The A43ΔCt mutant, which cannot form homodimers, shows 2-fold higher Pol I-Rrn3 levels and 6-fold increased promoter association in starved cells compared to wild-type, demonstrating that Pol I homodimerization is important for complete transcription inactivation upon starvation.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 provide PICT and ChIP data showing that preventing dimerization (via A43ΔCt) leads to incomplete clearance of Pol I-Rrn3 and maintained promoter association during starvation. The mutant has reduced growth (C34) but equivalent protein levels, making it a valid tool. The inference about dimerization's role in transcription inactivation (C39) is well-supported by the mutant phenotype.

results.result: Cryo-EM structures reveal monomeric Pol I at 4.9 Å resolution with a disordered, dynamic stalk and a half-closed cleft (38 Å width) representing an intermediate state between inactive dimeric and elongating Pol I.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 report the structural resolutions achieved. The observation of stalk disorder (C48) is directly supported by the density maps. The cleft width measurement (C50) is quantitative structural data. The interpretation of an intermediate state (C51) is reasonable based on comparison with known structures, though it involves some inference. The speculation about stalk dynamics' functional importance (C49) is appropriately qualified.

results.result: The Pol I-Rrn3 complex structure at 7.7 Å resolution shows that Rrn3 binds with its N-terminus facing the stalk, fixes the stalk position, and interacts primarily through A43 (OB domain with serine cradle) and A14 (helix α2 of TA domain) without inducing major conformational changes in Pol I.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are supported by antibody labeling and structural comparison. The lack of conformational changes (C54-C55) is demonstrated by structural superposition. The detailed interface analysis (C56-C58) is based on the cryo-EM density and is consistent with prior biochemical data (C57 cites Blattner et al., 2011). The 7.7 Å resolution is sufficient for these conclusions about domain interactions.

results.result: Mutational analysis of A14 reveals that helix α2 is fundamental for Rrn3 binding and promoter association (ΔA14 and A14-R91E show 75% reduction), while the TA-loop limits Rrn3 binding (A14ΔTAloop shows 2-fold increase). The A14 C-terminal tail is not involved in Rrn3 binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 provide PICT and ChIP data for multiple A14 mutants with consistent protein expression levels. The inference about helix α2's role (C62) is supported by convergent data from deletion and point mutants. The TA-loop's regulatory role (C63) is demonstrated by the opposite phenotype of A14ΔTAloop. The observation that higher Pol I-Rrn3 doesn't prevent dimerization or promoter dissociation in starved cells (C64) is an important control.

results.result: The dual repressive mechanism of Pol I-Rrn3 clearance and Pol I homodimerization is reversible upon nutrient addition, following a quasi-symmetric pattern that restores cell growth.
results.evaluation: Claim C42 demonstrates the symmetric pattern in time-course experiments. Claim C45 summarizes the differential adjustment of both complex types. Claim C5 connects this to growth restoration. The time-course data in Figure 4A clearly shows the reversibility, though the connection to growth restoration could be more directly demonstrated.

results.result: The Tub4-RFP-FKBP anchor increases PICT sensitivity by up to 200-fold compared to previously-engineered anchors by reducing the number of anchors to one or two per cell.
results.evaluation: Claim C17 is supported by direct comparison data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A. The quantification shows clear improvement in detection sensitivity. This is a methodological advance that enables the subsequent biological findings.

results.result: Pol III does not dimerize under growing or starving conditions, suggesting homodimerization is not a general mechanism for all nuclear RNA polymerases.
results.evaluation: Claim C25 is supported by PICT assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5. This negative result is important for establishing the specificity of Pol I dimerization. However, the authors appropriately note they cannot exclude Pol II/III dimerization under other conditions (C67).

results.result: Pol I-Rrn3 levels alone are insufficient to account for transcription inactivation, as complexes persist despite negligible promoter occupancy, suggesting additional regulatory mechanisms contribute to initial transcriptional inactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 identify an important discrepancy between complex levels and promoter occupancy. However, the evidence for 'additional regulatory mechanisms' (C72) is largely speculative. The proposed model (C73) about rapid recruitment upon refeeding is reasonable but not directly tested. This represents an important observation but requires additional experiments to identify the proposed additional mechanisms.

results.result: Pol I homodimerization may serve as a storage mechanism that protects the enzyme from degradation during starvation and enables rapid reactivation upon nutrient restoration without requiring de novo synthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 present a functional model for why dimerization occurs, but this is entirely speculative. No direct evidence is provided for protection from degradation or that stored dimers are preferentially used upon refeeding. While the model is plausible and consistent with the data, it requires experimental validation (e.g., degradation assays, pulse-chase experiments).

results.result: Structural comparison reveals that activating factors across different transcription systems (Pol I-Rrn3, Pol II-Mediator, bacterial σ factor) contact equivalent regions (stalk, dock domain, AC40/AC19 or homologs), suggesting a conserved architectural arrangement for enzyme activation and promoter recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 describe the Pol I-Rrn3 interface based on structural data. Claims C80-C85 cite literature for Pol II-Mediator and bacterial systems. The proposed conservation (C82, C86) involves significant speculation based on structural superposition. While the similarities are interesting, the functional significance of these analogies is not experimentally tested. The differences between systems may be as important as the similarities.
